input.rationale:
The observation already states that the paperwork shows the container was ventilated for the full period specified by the procedure and the placard has been struck through — this is the standard sign-off that ventilation per procedure was completed. So the fact the first pass bound its question to (whether the ventilation period was completed) is already established by the observation text; asking it again is not the decision-critical gap.

The real unresolved issue is different: this is fumigated hardwood flooring, tightly packed to the doors, and nobody has taken an atmospheric reading inside the load. Time-based ventilation (opening doors for a specified period) is a procedural proxy for the actual underlying hazard, which is residual fumigant gas concentration in a tightly packed load where off-gassing from dense wood stacked to the doors can trap pockets of gas even after the standard ventilation period has elapsed and the doors have been open. Given the load is tightly packed to the doors (poor air exchange within the stack) and no reading has been taken inside the load itself (only at/near the doors, presumably, if at all), the completion of the timed ventilation procedure does not by itself establish that the atmosphere is now safe to enter — that is precisely why atmospheric testing before entry into fumigated enclosed spaces is the standard control, independent of whether the nominal ventilation time has elapsed.

Branch A (a reading inside the load shows safe atmosphere) → picker may enter and unload.
Branch B (a reading inside the load shows unsafe atmosphere, e.g., residual fumigant trapped in the packed load despite door-opening) → keep picker out, do not unload, ventilate/test further.
These differ, and the answer is needed now because a picker is at the doors with a pallet truck about to enter/unload.

I therefore nominate this fact in addition to addressing the supplied fact. On the supplied fact itself, I find the observation already establishes completion of the timed procedure (paperwork + struck placard), so the property as named is effectively answered by the text, making the first-pass question redundant on that specific point — but I will flag this as a challenge rather than silently drop it, since the fact could still be read as open pending review.

input.rationale:
The property named — whether the replacement detection head will actually alarm on an ammonia release — is correctly the operative safety property, not a proxy: seeing the plant room as-is would not settle this because the head's response to a release cannot be observed by looking, only by a functional/gas check. The bound question ("Has the replacement detection head been bump tested or gas checked since it was fitted, and what did it read?") does reach this fact: an answer establishes whether verification occurred and what the result was, and a truthful 'no, not checked' answer leaves branch B's precautionary action in force, while a truthful 'yes, checked and reads correctly' supports branch A. So this fact is adequately covered by the first pass's own question.

However, the first pass's other question — about the fan's auto-start on gas alarm — addresses a second, separate control (the fan), and does not, on its own or together with the detection question, address a further necessary fact: whether ANY interim protection (continuous attendance, portable ammonia monitoring, or isolation/permit controls) is in place for the fitter who is about to break into the line right now, given that neither the bump test result nor the fan's auto-start status is yet known. The observation states a fitter is 'about to go in and break into the oil drain line' — an imminent entry into a space with an ammonia hazard whose detection is unverified and whose ventilation trigger is unconfirmed. Whether interim protective measures (attendance/portable monitoring/permit-to-work with isolation) are in place before that break-in is a fact that changes what is done RIGHT NOW: if such measures exist, the fitter may proceed under interim protection while the head/fan questions are chased up; if not, entry must be halted immediately regardless of the eventual bump-test answer, since a release during the break-in with no verified fixed detection and no interim monitoring is an immediate life-safety exposure. This is not covered by either supplied question, both of which ask about the state of fixed equipment rather than the interim protection accompanying the imminent task.

input.rationale: The observation states the guard "turns freely with it" (the shaft) and that nobody saw whether the retaining chain was reconnected. This leaves genuinely open whether the guard is restrained from rotating with the shaft. If restrained, the guard functions as intended and a worker can safely approach; if not, the guard itself becomes a rotating hazard rather than a protection, and the shaft must be stopped before contact. These lead to different actions today, so the fact is decision-critical. The first-pass question asks exactly this: "Is the power take-off guard retaining chain connected at the tractor end, and does the guard stay still when the shaft turns?" This is a conjunctive question that covers both the mechanism (chain connected) and the functional outcome (guard stays still) — an answer establishes both the physical restraint state and its functional consequence, which together settle the named property. The property named (whether the guard is restrained) is not a proxy for something else nor an adjacent property; it is exactly what governs whether approaching the rotating shaft is safe by hand, and it cannot be settled by mere sight since the guard turning freely with the shaft is consistent with both a reconnected chain that simply hasn't been visually verified as taut, or a genuinely disconnected chain — an unseen state that could go either way. The "held while unresolved" action (stop the shaft) is appropriately conservative and does not presume either branch. I do not find any other fact not already supplied that would change what is done today: the tractor idling, the worker's intent to move the spout by hand, and the guard's free rotation are all stated plainly and do not introduce a second decision-critical unknown beyond the one already identified.

input.rationale: The named property (whether the bay will hold a person leaning against it) is the real safety property, but the bound question is not adequately sufficient and the "what is done meanwhile" clause presumes a branch. The question offers an alternative ("or what does the bay do under a load test") which is answered by whichever branch is easiest: an answer stating a torque value in foot-pounds does not by itself establish that the bay will hold a person leaning against it (structural adequacy requires knowing the specified/required torque for that connection, not just a number). The weaker branch of the "or" — merely stating what torque was applied — does not settle the load-bearing property unless compared against a required spec, which is not established anywhere in the observation. So as currently written, an answer under the torque branch could be truthfully given without establishing adequacy. I am replacing/tightening the clarification to require it to reach the actual property: whether the bay currently supports the required load (by load test or by verification against the specified torque), and treat "picking continues on the basis the rail is sound" as an unresolved-action framing that must be corrected — since a rail whose fastening method is literally unknown, on an edge-protection feature protecting a fall hazard, is exactly the case where an unverified control cannot be treated as equivalent to a checked one. The clarification must ask for the load-bearing status directly, not merely the torque figure standing alone.

proposedClarification.question: Has the replaced bay of edge protection rail been verified — by load test, or by confirming the bolts were torqued to the specified value for that connection — to currently hold the required load (e.g., a person leaning or falling against it), and until that verification, has picking along this face been stopped or the bay barricaded?
proposedClarification.whyItMatters: The observation states only that the bolts are in and the rail looks in line, and explicitly that nobody can say whether the bolts were torqued or just run up by hand. A rail bolted finger-tight will not resist a fall load the way a properly torqued rail will, and this is a fall-protection control on an elevated pick face where pickers are actively working now. Whether the bay currently meets its load-bearing requirement determines whether picking may continue along this face or must stop until the rail is made good.
proposedClarification.evidenceGap: Whether the replaced bay's fastening is currently sufficient to bear the required edge-protection load has not been checked by anyone; only its visual alignment and bolt presence were observed.
